summary: Defines how to carry MPEG-4 audio and video streams in RTP packets without using MPEG-4 Systems. It obsoletes RFC 3016, fixing a mismatch with the 3GPP streaming specification for MPEG-4 audio, and it summarizes the changes and compatibility.

eli5.summary: Video and sound are big, so they are cut into small packets for sending over the internet. This explains how to slice and label MPEG-4 audio and video so the receiver can piece them back together.

subtitle: How to put MPEG-4 audio and video straight into RTP packets, without MPEG-4 Systems.

tldr.problem: Systems such as H.323, SIP and RTSP manage streams themselves and need a way to carry MPEG-4 Audio and Visual data in RTP without the MPEG-4 Systems layer. RFC 3016 had drifted out of line with the 3GPP streaming specification.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps MPEG-4 Visual bitstreams and LATM-formatted MPEG-4 Audio directly onto RTP payloads, sets rules for RTP header fields and fragmentation, and defines the media types and SDP parameters to describe the streams.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3016 and corrects the LATM version, the SBR 'rate' definition and related signaling. The RFC itself advises new system designs to use RFC 3640 for audio.

today: RFC 6416 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 3016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its own abstract advises new system designs to use RFC 3640 for audio.

sections.title: Carrying MPEG-4 Without MPEG-4 Systems
sections.content:
This RFC specifies how MPEG-4 Audio and MPEG-4 Visual streams are fragmented and mapped directly onto RTP packets, without the synchronization and stream management of MPEG-4 Systems. It is meant for systems that already manage streams themselves. The RFC names H.323 terminals (which use H.245) and SIP and RTSP (which use media types and SDP) as examples.

The stated benefit is that these formats can be handled in the same way as payload formats for non-MPEG-4 codecs. The stated disadvantage is that interoperability with environments using MPEG-4 Systems may be difficult, so other payload formats may suit those better.

For video, no extra RTP header fields are defined, because MPEG-4 Visual already has its own error resiliency tools for recovering corrupt headers. For audio, a single audio frame per payload means a lost packet does not harm the decodability of its neighbors. Existing protections such as Generic Forward Error Correction (RFC 5109) and Redundant Audio Data (RFC 2198) MAY be applied.
sections.eli5: Some systems already keep track of their own video and sound. This RFC lets them drop MPEG-4 pictures and sound into network packets directly, like putting letters straight into envelopes with no extra paperwork.

sections.title: Audio Configuration and LATM Restrictions
sections.content:
For MPEG-4 Audio, the decoder's output can differ from the core codec configuration when Spectral Band Replication (SBR) or Parametric Stereo (PS) is used. With SBR the output sampling rate is typically double the core rate, except in down-sampled SBR mode. With PS the core codec is mono but the final output is stereo.

Audio is carried in LATM, the Low-overhead MPEG-4 Audio Transport Multiplex. Two LATM features, multiplexing multiple objects (programs) and multiplexing scalable layers, MUST NOT be used. Structured Audio and Text-to-Speech Interface data MUST NOT be carried either, since LATM was built only for natural audio coding tools.

For scalable streams, each layer SHOULD go in its own RTP stream. The dependency between layers SHOULD be signaled as specified in RFC 5583.
sections.eli5: Some audio tricks make a small recording sound bigger when played back. Because of this, the numbers in the packets describe the small recording, not the final sound.

sections.title: Packetizing MPEG-4 Visual
sections.content:
An MPEG-4 Visual bitstream goes straight into the RTP payload, with no extra header fields and nothing removed. The Combined Configuration/Elementary stream mode MUST be used. When the short video header mode is used, the H.263 payload format SHOULD be used instead, with RFC 4629 recommended.

The marker bit is 1 on the last (or only) RTP packet of a Video Object Plane (VOP). The timestamp gives the sampling instance of the VOP, with a default resolution of 90 kHz unless set out of band. Sequence numbers go up by 1 per packet and start from a random value.

The fragmentation rules are:

  • Configuration information and Group_of_VideoObjectPlane() SHALL come at the start of the payload or just after the header of a higher-level function.
  • The payload SHALL begin with the header of the syntactically highest function it contains.
  • A header SHALL NOT be split across RTP packets.
  • Different VOPs SHOULD go in different packets, though several small consecutive VOPs MAY share one.
  • A single video packet SHOULD be sent as a single RTP packet no larger than the Path MTU. If video packets are disabled by setting resync_marker_disable to 1, a VOP MAY be split at arbitrary byte positions.

The RFC illustrates the trade-off: one video packet per RTP packet is recommended when loss is high, while several per packet saves header overhead on low-bitrate networks but loses more at once if a packet is dropped.
sections.eli5: A video frame is cut into pieces that each carry a clear start. Cut at the sensible places, and a lost piece does not ruin the others.

sections.title: Packetizing MPEG-4 Audio
sections.content:
MPEG-4 Audio streams MUST be LATM streams. A complete audioMuxElement, or a part of one, SHALL be mapped directly onto the RTP payload, and its first byte SHALL be at the first payload position. The RTP header sits in front of it as normal.

The muxConfigPresent setting must be known out of band; in SDP it corresponds to the cpresent parameter. When it is 1 (in-band mode), the element includes a useSameStreamMux bit and MAY include the StreamMuxConfig. Because a lost earlier frame can make a later one undecodable, the StreamMuxConfig SHOULD be sent repeatedly. When it is 0, the configuration travels out of band, for example in the SDP config parameter.

The marker bit is 1 when the packet holds a complete audioMuxElement or its last fragment. The timestamp is the sampling instance of the first audio frame in the packet, with a default resolution of 90 kHz. It is RECOMMENDED to put one audioMuxElement in each packet, and if it would exceed the Path MTU, it SHALL be fragmented across packets.
sections.eli5: Audio is sent as chunks, with a marker saying where each full chunk ends. A setup note tells the receiver how to play them, and it is repeated in case one copy gets lost.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
Video is registered as video/MP4V-ES. Its optional parameters are rate (timestamp resolution, default 90000), profile-level-id (default 1, Simple Profile/Level 1) and config (the hexadecimal configuration information, which SHALL be used to describe the stream).

Audio is registered as audio/MP4A-LATM. rate is required, with a default of 90000, and other values MAY be used only if equal to the audio sampling rate. With SBR the rate is not the definitive sampling rate. Optional parameters include profile-level-id (default 30), object, bitrate, cpresent (default 1), config, MPS-asc, ptime and SBR-enabled.

Both map into SDP: the media type goes in m=, the subtype in a=rtpmap, and the other parameters in a=fmtp as semicolon-separated pairs. Receivers MUST ignore any unspecified parameter so that future ones can be added.
sections.eli5: These are the labels on the box that tell the other side what is inside: video or audio, how it was packed, and how to open it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The packets are subject to the security considerations of RTP and of any applicable RTP profile. The main concerns are confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity. No one mechanism fits every case, though the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) is recommended where suitable. IPsec and TLS are named as other options.

MPEG-4 codecs usually have an extension mechanism whose extra data decoders skip, and it could be used to carry unwanted data in an otherwise valid stream. The RFC also finds no significant non-uniformity in receiver complexity, so denial of service from pathological data is unlikely. Because the format covers only audio and video, MPEG-J applets and scripts from full MPEG-4 Systems cannot be carried.
sections.eli5: To keep the stream private and untampered, use a secure wrapper. And since only sound and pictures can ride in these packets, no hidden programs can sneak in.

sections.title: Differences From RFC 3016
sections.content:
RFC 3016 was used by the 3GPP Packet-switched Streaming Service, but the two were misaligned. This update fixes that:

  • It references the newer LATM format, binary compatible with 3GPP but not with the LATM referenced in RFC 3016.
  • The StreamMuxConfig format is aligned with 3GPP.
  • The SBR-enabled parameter is defined; RFC 3016 did not have it.
  • The rate parameter is defined unambiguously when SBR is present, and the channel count when PS is present.
  • Signaling support for MPEG Surround is added.

Requirement changes include: a different payload type per layer for scalable audio, signaling layer dependencies per RFC 5583, a requirement to fragment oversized audioMuxElements, and a rule that receivers MUST ignore unspecified parameters.
sections.eli5: An older rulebook did not quite match what phones were doing. This is the corrected edition that lines them up.

sections.title: Compatibility and Relation to RFC 3640
sections.content:
This specification is not backwards compatible with RFC 3016, because it mandates a binary incompatible LATM version. Implementations that use the LATM version from RFC 3016 MUST be updated to comply. Existing implementations using a recent LATM version may already comply with this document.

The audio signaling here is less explicit than in RFC 3640, which the abstract says new system designs should use because it lacks the restrictions on signaling audio codec parameters. The RFC argues that the use of LATM in various transmission standards still justifies this revision.
sections.eli5: The new version cannot be read by old equipment that follows the old rules, so that equipment has to be updated.
